card werk-mc-live-bgcount  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
A tab counts its background tasks from the last full list its agent sent
why: The agent sends its whole list of background tasks each time one starts or ends. Werk keeps the length of the last list, so one lost event cannot leave a wrong count. A count of starts and ends would stay wrong after one lost event, and the tab would never read as idle again.

A background task is a subagent or a shell command that the agent starts and that runs on after its turn ends. Claude Code, the agent that werk runs in each tab, sends the full list of these tasks each time one starts or ends. To avoid a count that drifts after one lost event, werk does not add up starts and ends. It replaces the tab's count with the length of each new list. This count is what keeps a tab with a finished turn marked as running (see #werk-mc-bgagents). When the tab's child process exits, its tasks end with it, and the count goes to zero.

Example:
- tab #fold "Fold the cards from the log"
- task A, a subagent that reviews a card
- task B, a shell command that runs the tests

1. The agent starts task A and sends the list [A]. The count is 1.
2. The agent starts task B and sends [A, B]. The count is 2.
3. The turn ends. The count is 2, so #fold still shows as running.
4. Task A ends, but werk loses the list [B]. The count stays 2.
5. Task B ends, and the agent sends []. The count is 0, and #fold is idle. The lost list in step 4 leaves no error.
6. Any other event from the agent leaves the count as it is.
7. If the child exits while a task runs, the count goes to 0 at once.

```
  list from the agent       count   #fold chip
  [A]                       1       running
  [A, B]                    2       running
  (turn ends)               2       running
  [B]  -- lost --           2       running
  []                        0       idle

  count = number of tasks in the last list received
  child exits               0       (dead or idle, never running)
```

Resumed session af7c5b98.

In normal use, the two give the same number. They differ in what one event does:

| | Last list (the card) | Count starts and ends (`:opt0`) |
|---|---|---|
| What werk stores | One number | One number, plus the id of each running task |
| What one event does | It sets the count to the length of the list | It adds 1 or subtracts 1 |
| Does an event depend on the earlier ones? | No | Yes. Each event changes the result of all the earlier ones |
| An event werk skips | The next list corrects the count | The count stays wrong until the child exits |
| An event werk reads twice | No effect | The count is off by one |

```
events:     [A]   [A,B]   [B]   (skipped)   []
last list:   1      2      1        1        0   ← correct again at the next list
start/end:  +1     +1     -1        -       0?   ← each step needs the step before it
```

The agent already sends the full list. So the start/end option makes werk rebuild a number that the agent gives it directly.

The card is a small decision. It is one module's choice, and both options give the same visible result. You have two choices:

1. Accept it as is. It records why the count cannot drift.
2. Drop it, and add one sentence to `#werk-mc-bgagents`: "the count is the length of the last task list the agent sent."

I recommend option 2, because rule 6 keeps one module's details off the map.

card werk-wording  [decided]
A card's words describe its own subject, not the session that wrote it
why: A card is read later, cold, by someone who needs to act on its subject. Session facts (who said what, what came before, what stage the conversation was at) are stale on arrival and carry no decision weight.

No planning-process narration in a title, why, or body: no "Eryk said", no "the next thing to prove", no comparison to where the conversation stands.

This includes a card's own edit history. "X is new", "Y used to say/name Z", "that no longer holds/applies" still narrate the session, even when the subject is the card itself. State the current fact plainly. The same holds for where the text came from: "moved here from #x", "split out of #y", "merged from #z". The log records the move; the card states the fact.

A reversal is still fair game to record — a superseded card can say what replaced it and why the earlier reading was wrong — but as a fact about the subject, not a play-by-play of the conversation that produced it. Attribution lives in the "who" field and in the log, not in prose.

A card stays at the level of the decision. It names behaviour and concepts. It does not name a command or a flag: the command form of an operation lives on one card under #werk-cli, and every other card names the operation instead. It does not name source files, functions, classes, constants, line numbers, or internal endpoints. Those change with every refactor, and the card would go stale while its decision still holds. The code points to the card, not the other way round.

The map records decisions that hold for any module, not results for one module. Applying a rule to one module — its behaviour list, its coverage threshold, its test plan — produces an artifact, not a decision. That artifact lives next to the code it describes, in the module's own tests. A card for one module is fair only when that module raises a real design fork the general rule cannot settle.

A card does not list its child cards. The refines edges hold that list, and the map draws it under the card. A copy in the body is a second list that catches up only later: a child that is added, moved, or removed leaves the copy wrong, and no mark shows it. A card states its own higher-level fact. When a sentence states a fact that a child card expands, it names that child in parentheses after the fact. A bullet list or a numbered list in a body is a last resort in general. A list whose items mirror the children is never correct, even when each item is a short fact with the child in parentheses.

The tab's live marker counts a background agent as running too (see #werk-mc-live). So a tab whose turn has ended does not read as idle while its background agent works (#werk-mc-live-bgcount gives the count).

Example:

- tab #fold "Fold the cards from the log"
- agent R, a background subagent that reviews a card

1. A turn in #fold starts R, and the turn ends. The #fold pane shows the line, and the #fold chip still shows running.
2. R ends. The line goes, and the chip shows idle.
3. A turn that starts no background agent shows no line at any time.
